The Brecon Beacons: South Wales' Riding Treasure

Now officially renamed Bannau Brycheiniog, the Brecon Beacons remain one of Wales' finest motorcycle destinations. The park stretches across South Wales from the Black Mountains in the east to the Black Mountain in the west, offering varied riding through mountain, moorland, and river valley landscapes.

The Black Mountain Road (A4069)

The A4069 is the Brecon Beacons' undisputed highlight and one of Britain's finest motorcycle roads. Starting from Llandovery, the road climbs across open moorland with perfectly cambered sweeping bends. The descent towards Brynamman features tight hairpins with views across the Towy Valley. This road has appeared in car and motorcycle magazines countless times, and it lives up to the hype.

Waterfall Country

The Ystradfellte area in the southern Beacons is known as Waterfall Country. Four major waterfalls cascade through wooded gorges, the most famous being Sgwd yr Eira, where you can walk behind the falling water. The roads approaching Waterfall Country through the Neath Valley are steep and wooded — atmospheric riding.

The Gospel Pass

The Gospel Pass above Hay-on-Wye is one of Wales' best-kept secrets. This narrow, unfenced mountain road climbs to 549 metres through the Black Mountains with views across the English border. The descent to Llanthony Priory (a ruined medieval priory with a hotel built into the ruins) is one of the most atmospheric rides in Wales.

The Brecon Beacons offer the best motorcycle roads in South Wales. The Black Mountain Road alone justifies a visit, but there's much more to explore beyond the headline act.

Best Routes

  • A4069 Black Mountain — The signature road, flowing bends across open moorland
  • A470 through the Beacons — The park's spine road, dramatic mountain scenery
  • A4059 Aberdare to Brecon — Climbs from the Valleys to the mountain plateau
  • Minor road over the Epynt — Military range road (open most weekends), wild and empty

Practical Information

The main towns — Brecon, Abergavenny, and Merthyr Tydfil — all have fuel, accommodation, and services. The park is easily accessible from Cardiff (1 hour), Bristol (1.5 hours), and Birmingham (2 hours). Weather is changeable — the Beacons attract rainfall, especially on the western side. The best months are May-September, with June being particularly good for wild flowers on the moorland. Hay-on-Wye, the town of bookshops, is a charming base on the eastern edge.

faq.q: What is the best road in the Brecon Beacons?
faq.a: The A4069 Black Mountain Road is the undisputed highlight and one of Britain's finest motorcycle roads. Starting from Llandovery, it climbs across open moorland with perfectly cambered sweeping bends, then descends towards Brynamman with tight hairpins and views across the Towy Valley. It alone justifies a visit to the park.

The Gospel Pass above Hay-on-Wye is Wales' highest road at 549 metres and one of the country's best-kept secrets. This narrow, unfenced mountain road climbs through the Black Mountains with views across the English border, then descends to Llanthony Priory, a ruined medieval priory with a hotel built into the ruins.

faq.q: Where can I get fuel and stay?
faq.a: The main towns of Brecon, Abergavenny and Merthyr Tydfil all have fuel, accommodation and services. Hay-on-Wye, the town of bookshops on the eastern edge, makes a charming base. The park is easily reached from Cardiff in about an hour, Bristol in 1.5 hours and Birmingham in two hours.

faq.q: When is the best time to ride here?
faq.a: The best months are May to September, with June particularly good for wild flowers on the moorland. Weather is changeable, as the Beacons attract rainfall, especially on the western side, so carry waterproofs. Some routes, such as the Epynt military range road, are only open most weekends.

faq.q: What else is worth seeing beyond the roads?
faq.a: Waterfall Country around Ystradfellte in the southern Beacons has four major waterfalls flowing through wooded gorges, the most famous being Sgwd yr Eira, where you can walk behind the falling water. The approach roads through the Neath Valley are steep, wooded and atmospheric.
